The problem is the ISO: .126 at A, translating to .099 at the MLB level against a landscape where .150 is ordinary, which means the on-base skill has to do most of the carrying if he's ever to be more than an organizational piece. If the gap power never fills in as he physically matures, you're looking at a bench bat with a good eye and 28 stolen bases, nothing worse but nothing more.

829037_hitter.text: The contact rate is the whole argument here, and it's pointing the right direction. Across 384 plate appearances at A, Kevin Alvarez is striking out at an 18% clip, tidy for an 18-year-old, but the MLB-equivalent translation comes out to 23.2%, which leaves almost no cushion. The .168 ISO at A translates to .118 at the MLB level, and that gap is where the ceiling closes. Everything hinges on whether the bat-to-ball feel develops enough to lift a walk rate that currently translates to 7.7%, below what the average MLB hitter draws, and if it doesn't, what's left is a depth outfielder rather than a regular.

829052_hitter.text: Breyson Guedez is a young left-handed hitter working through strikeout noise at the A level, flashing contact ability (.282 avg, 83rd percentile) but generating minimal power (.119 ISO, 31st percentile) and very little leverage on base (6.6% BB rate, 8th percentile). At 18 with only 272 plate appearances, the strikeout rate (29%) sits just above major-league average in the translation, a concerning baseline for someone still learning pitch recognition. The hit tool is real, but without secondary skills or early power development, the path to impact is narrow.

829058_hitter.text: Gabriel Davalillo is an 18-year-old third baseman showing mixed bat discipline and pop: he's posting .267/.348/.410 with an 11% walk rate and .143 ISO over 227 A-ball plate appearances, though both his strikeout rate (25.6%) and isolated power rank near the middle of the minor-league field. The real concern is that his average and slugging power lag below the tools expected at the position—his .267 AVG is strong for his age, but ISO in the 47th percentile signals he hasn't yet connected the bat to game power. The sample is current and meaningful, but at 18 with moderate command and modest thump so far, this looks like a years-away organizational depth profile rather than a near-term contributor.

829210_hitter.text: Ty Harvey is a 19-year-old catcher showing early discipline at the plate—19% BB% on a 58 PA sample—but swinging and missing at a concerning clip (24.1% K%). His .107 ISO translates to below-average raw power for a catcher, and the strikeout rate (24.1%), even accounting for youth, sits above league average in the MLB equivalent read. The sample is small and fresh, so expect volatility as he faces stiffer velocity and sequencing.

829854_hitter.text: Luis Arana is an 18-year-old A-level shortstop who commands the strike zone exceptionally—posting 19.2% BB% over 78 PA—but whose overall bat lacks impact, evidenced by a modest .127 ISO and a .460 SLG despite the strong .462 OBP. The approach grade is elite relative to his peer group; the hit tool is solid; but power and overall impact are well below average, and that power ceiling is the central constraint. At 78 plate appearances in a current season sample, confidence in the profile is limited, though the plate discipline suggests a repeatable skill.

830239_hitter.text: The ISO is the argument: .243 at A+ over 331 plate appearances, which translates to .159 at the MLB level, right at league average for raw power despite coming from a 22-year-old center fielder. The .885 OPS and 15 home runs alongside 18 stolen bases make the impact grade look earned, not fluky. What complicates it is the 27% strikeout rate, because that translates to 29.5% against big-league pitching, and a hit tool that grades 55 can carry a 27% K-rate in the minors long before it can carry one against advanced arms. If the contact holds, Walton profiles as a low-end everyday regular with speed-and-power upside; if pitchers find the hole, what's left is a bench bat with real pop.

830336_pitcher.text: A 1.3 ERA and a 0.8 WHIP across A+ & A in 2026 are the kind of numbers that make you stop scrolling, and the 29% K-BB% sitting at the 99th percentile of his pitcher pool makes the underlying case that this isn't just soft contact luck. His 74 strikeouts in 53.6 innings translate to an 8.4 K/9 equivalent at the MLB level, landing right at league average, and that's the ceiling conversation in one number. The command is genuine, a 2.2 BB/9 that translates to 3.0 at the MLB level where the typical starter sits at 3.2, but if the strikeout rate doesn't hold up against better hitters, the floor is a depth arm with functional control and not much else.

830402_pitcher.text: A 0.9 WHIP at 18 years old, across A+ & A, turns heads before you look at anything else. Kendry Chourio has walked 15 batters in 81.7 innings, a 1.7 BB/9 that sits at the 99th percentile of his pool, and the translation shows his command profile carries forward even if the strikeout rate lands at 7.1 per nine in MLB-equivalent terms, noticeably softer than his present dominance suggests. The profile hinges entirely on that control: if it holds as he climbs, there's a real pitcher in here; if hitters at higher levels expose a strikeout rate that's already thin, the floor is depth arm and not much else.

832562_pitcher.text: The K-BB% is the loudest number here: 23% across A+ & A, which translates to 13.7% in MLB context, right at league average, though you'd never guess it from how the raw strikeout rate pops. Dylan Brown is punching out 126 batters in 92 innings, a 12.3 K/9 that softens considerably in translation to 8.8, and the walk rate tells a similar story, 3.5 per nine in the minors becoming 3.9 against big-league competition. The ceiling here is a depth arm, the floor is a depth arm, and the whole bet is whether the strikeout shape holds enough through the levels to keep that K-BB% propped up once the walks stop being cheap.

834962_hitter.text: Seventeen home runs across AA & A+ in 370 plate appearances, with 48 walks against 79 strikeouts, is a bat-first first baseman profile that carries real weight at Double-A. The .218 ISO translates to .156 against MLB pitching, and the translated 10.2% walk rate clears the MLB average of 8.5%, so the approach adds something even after the level discount. A 13% walk rate and .378 OBP suggest someone who can put a lineup together rather than just feast on minor-league arms. If the contact, 21% strikeouts and .266 average, survives the jump, DePino is a low-end everyday regular at first; if it doesn't, the power alone leaves a useful bench bat.

834978_pitcher.text: The surface numbers are loud: 11.0 K/9, a 1.1 WHIP, a K-BB% that ranks 90th among the pitcher pool across AA & A+. Translate those 96 innings to MLB-equivalent context and the profile goes quiet fast, with a K/9 of 8.5 sitting right at league average and a BB/9 of 3.6 that runs a tick above it. The stuff plays up in the minors in a way it probably won't against a big-league lineup. If the command tightens and the strikeout rate holds its shape at that level, he's a backend arm who eats innings; if neither translates, what's left is a depth piece competing for a roster spot.
